title: Flip Every Block of k
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list and a number k. Cut the list into consecutive blocks of k nodes, starting from the head, and reverse the nodes inside each block. Return the new head.

If the last block has fewer than k nodes, leave it in its original order.

Relink the existing nodes; do not just rewrite their values. Lists are written as arrays: [5, 10] is 5 → 10.

examples.why: Two full blocks of three are flipped. The last two nodes form a short block, so 14 → 16 stays as it is.
Each flipped block has to be linked to the next flipped block: 5, the old first node of block one, now points at 20, the new first node of block two.
One full block, then a leftover of one node that is not touched.

hints: You already know how to reverse a whole list. What extra information do you need to reverse just k nodes and plug them back in?
Before reversing a block, check that k nodes are actually there. For each block, keep track of the node right before it and the node right after it.

Use a dummy node before the head as the first "node before the block". Reverse the k nodes, then connect the node before the block to the new block start, and the old block start (now its end) to the node after the block. That old start is the "node before" for the next block.

explain.intuition:
Each block is a small "reverse a list" problem. The hard part is the wiring at the edges. When you reverse a block, its first node becomes its last, and its last becomes its first. So two links must be fixed: the node before the block must now point at the block's old last node, and the block's old first node must point at whatever comes after the block.

Keep a pointer groupPrev to the node before the current block, starting at a dummy node in front of the head so that the first block is not a special case. Before touching anything, walk k steps to make sure a full block exists; if not, stop and leave the rest alone. After the flip, the block's old first node is its new last node, and it becomes groupPrev for the next block.
steps: Create dummy with dummy.next = head, and set groupPrev = dummy.
Find the k-th node after groupPrev. If the list ends first, stop.
Let after = kth.next. Reverse the nodes from groupPrev.next to kth, starting with prev = after so the reversed block's tail already points onward.
Save first = groupPrev.next (the old first, now last), set groupPrev.next = kth, then set groupPrev = first.
pitfalls: Reversing the short final block too. Always count k nodes before you change any pointer.
Forgetting to reconnect: the node before a block still points at the old first node, which is now the block's last node, so whole blocks vanish from the result.
Moving groupPrev to kth instead of the old first node. After the flip, kth is at the front of the block, not the end.

solutions.title: Reverse values block by block, rebuild
solutions.idea: Copy the values into an array, reverse each full block of k in the array, and build a new list. Easy to reason about, but it uses O(n) memory and creates new nodes.

solutions.title: Reverse in place, block by block
solutions.idea: Keep the node before the current block. Check k nodes exist, reverse them so the block's tail points to the node after the block, then hook the block's new head onto the node before it.

followups: Reverse the short final block as well. Which check do you remove?
Reverse only every other block of k and leave the blocks in between alone.
